<reason>B fought the more inventive and often sharper battle: the asymmetric-power dissolution of A's contradiction charge, the Goodhart turn on A's posted-quota concession, and the fraud-exemption trap were the flashiest moves of the debate. But B's path to victory required substituting "disclosure vs. substantive reform" for the motion as written, and A's pressure Q1 forced the concession that the motion blocks nothing — leaving B's crowding-out case resting on speculative legislative politics. Meanwhile A's regulator-level route (subpoena targets, proactive cross-firm registry, falsity liability, "entry powers locate the door, not what's behind it") was never squarely neutralized, and A showed B's tribunal alternative borrows disclosure's premise while being individual, retrospective, and settlement-sealed. B never defended secrecy on the merits and never answered the proactive-enforcement point in its closing. A's slightly cleaner path through the actual decision rule, plus B's clipped rebuttal as a minor execution cost, gives A a razor-thin but real edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q1 on the fraud exemption — catching A's threshold-exemption concession and applying it to A's own deactivated driver, crystallized in B4.6 as "gives him the fact he had and withholds the fact he needs" — was the single most damaging hit, though A's A1 recovery (existence, data categories, clustering audits, false-filing liability) kept the systemic case alive.</best_rebuttal>
